introduction: The study tests whether positive mental health mediates the link between physical activity and depressive symptoms among college students. Depressive symptoms are described as a pressing global public health challenge and the most prevalent mental health disorder among college students.
methodology: Cross-sectional online survey of 3,140 Chinese college students, recruited by convenience sampling between May and June 2025 and aged 18–27. Measures were the PARS-3 (α = 0.634), the Positive Mental Health Scale (α = 0.95) and the PHQ-9 (α = 0.935). Analysis used Spearman correlations and PROCESS Model 4 with 5,000 bootstrap resamples, controlling for age, gender, grade and educational level.
theory: The study is anchored in Self-Determination Theory, which names autonomy, competence and relatedness as three innate psychological needs critical to high-quality motivation and psychological well-being.
results: Physical activity was significantly associated with depressive symptoms in total (c = −0.015, p < 0.01). The indirect effect through positive mental health was significant (ab = −0.007, 95% CI [−0.010, −0.004]), while the direct effect was not significant (c' = −0.008, p = 0.080). Positive mental health was negatively associated with depressive symptoms (b = −0.250, p < 0.001).
discussion: The authors read the results as a small indirect association consistent with a mediation pattern, with positive mental health as a possible mediator. They propose positive mental health as a useful conceptual focus for future research and a multi-tiered strategy for colleges to integrate physical activity into mental health promotion.
limitations: The authors note that the cross-sectional design prevents confirmation of causal sequences, that self-reported positive mental health may not capture culturally distinct well-being, that PARS-3 reliability was modest (α = 0.634), that convenience sampling limits generalizability, and that the variance explained was low (R2 = 0.014). Suggested directions include longitudinal experience-sampling studies, mixed-methods work, PARS-3 validation, replication in probabilistic samples and cross-cultural validation.

abstract_claims.q: Numerous studies confirm that physical activity alleviates depressive symptoms in college students, but the underlying mechanisms remain unclear.
Results showed 69.39% of participants had low physical activity, and 19.24% reported clinically significant depressive symptoms.
The findings showed significant correlations among the three variables, with positive mental health strongly associated with reduced depressive symptoms.
Bootstrap mediation analysis (5,000 iterations) confirmed a mediating role of positive mental health.
This study advances theoretical understanding by identifying positive mental health as one possible pathway linking physical activity to better mental health outcomes.
Due to the effect is small, the results should be interpreted cautiously.

The findings provide conceptual support for integrating positive mental health promotion into physical activity-based interventions targeting college students’ depressive symptoms, with no causal inferences implied due to the cross-sectional design.
